$comment: DRAFTED BY THE BUILD, NOT APPROVED BY AN OWNER. `approval.approved_by_subject` is null, so nothing loads this into oe.category_rubrics and CE-CONTENT-01 and CE-VISUAL-01 stay unrequestable — the same arrangement as config/offer-approvals.json, where an unpriced SKU stays unsellable rather than defaulting to sellable. This file exists so the argument can be had against something concrete instead of against a blank page. See docs/adr/ADR-027-category-rubric.md.
$what_I_am_least_sure_about: visual.minimum_product_images = 3. This is the weakest number in the file. Three (front, back, detail) is the conventional floor for apparel, but I have not counted a sample of shops that convert well against a sample that does not, and neither has anybody else here. It is a convention I am repeating, not a measurement.

Whether `returns_window` belongs in `required` at all. A buyer will not refuse to buy an overshirt because the returns window is not restated on the product page — they assume the EU statutory right exists, and it does. I kept it required because fit is the single largest return driver in apparel and an unstated policy is what turns a return into a complaint, but a reasonable colleague would move it to `expected` and I would not fight hard.

Whether a linked size guide counts as the page stating measurements. I said yes (`may_be_on_a_linked_page: true`) because that is how most competent shops do it. Somebody who believes measurements must be on the page itself would get a very different defect rate out of the same rubric, and the rubric would still look reasonable to them.

The German patterns are mine, not a native merchant's. `Zusammensetzung` and `Materialzusammensetzung` are right; I am less sure I have the common spellings a small DACH shop actually uses, and a missed spelling reads as a missing disclosure, which is a false positive against a page that did nothing wrong.

category.label: Everyday layers — overshirts, jackets, knitwear, sold direct to consumer
category.why_this_one: It is the only category this build has ever inspected: every fixture in fixtures/m2-server.mjs is an 'Everyday overshirt', and both ventures that would sell a scan sell into DACH apparel. Proving the rubric anywhere else would mean proving it against pages nobody here has seen.

content.$comment: CE-CONTENT-01 · 'Category-specific buying information not found in disclosed inspected sample after module/link checks'. Each item is something a page either says or does not say. IMPORTANT: this checks that the page states something about the item, not that what it states is adequate. A page reading 'Material: siehe Etikett' passes. That limitation is carried in every finding rather than corrected here, because judging adequacy is a reader's job and this rule does not have a reader.

required.why_required: Fibre content decides whether a garment is warm, whether it itches, and whether the buyer can wash it. It is also mandatory disclosure for textiles sold in the EU under Regulation 1007/2011, so a page without it is not merely unhelpful.

A size letter is not a measurement, and an S from one shop is an M from another. Fit uncertainty is the largest single cause of apparel returns, and a buyer who cannot resolve it either does not buy or buys two sizes intending to send one back.

required.question_a_buyer_asks: What happens if it does not fit?
required.why_required: Fit cannot be settled before delivery, so in this category the returns term is part of the purchase decision rather than after-sales detail. See the caveat in $what_I_am_least_sure_about: this is the item most likely to belong one rung lower.

expected.question_a_buyer_asks: How does it sit on somebody my size?

contested: Whether a fit description — 'relaxed fit', 'true to size', 'fällt klein aus' — is buying information or copywriting. It changes purchase decisions, which argues for required; it is also unverifiable and unfalsifiable, which argues for never claiming it.

Whether sustainability and provenance claims belong in the rubric. 'Made in Portugal' is decisive for one buyer and noise to another, and a rule that treats its absence as a defect is enforcing a house style on somebody else's shop.

Whether a returns term has to be numeric. 'Free returns' with no window says less than '14 Tage' but reads as more generous, and deciding which counts as stated is a judgement about the merchant's honesty, not about the page.

Stock and availability. Deliberately absent: CE-DATA-01 already compares declared availability against what the page shows, and two rules claiming one defect would put the same problem in front of a reviewer twice under different names.

Price transparency — whether VAT and shipping basis must be stated on the product page. Left out here because CE-DATA-01 owns the price surface, but a reasonable person would say the rubric is incomplete without it.

visual.$comment: CE-VISUAL-01 · 'Real image sequence fails a specific category buying-question rubric; specialist review'. This rule cannot see what is IN a photograph — there is no vision model in this system, and adding one would mean a machine asserting what a picture shows. It can count images and read what the page declares about them. Everything that needs an eye is under `needs_a_human` and is recorded as an open question, never as a finding.

required_shots.question_a_buyer_asks: What does the whole garment look like?
What does the material actually look like up close?
What does the back look like?
How does it hang on a person?

needs_a_human: Whether the colour shown is the colour that arrives. The most common and most expensive apparel complaint, and nothing in a captured page can answer it.
Whether the garment is photographed on a body or laid flat. Alt text almost never says, and guessing from a filename would be a fabricated observation.
Whether the images show this product or a stock photograph of something similar.
Whether scale is readable — a knit that photographs like a fine gauge and arrives chunky is a return, and no count of images detects it.

approval.$comment: Mirrors config/offer-approvals.json. A rubric is used only when an owner has signed it, and this file records who and when. Null here is not a placeholder to be filled in casually: it is the reason both detectors are currently unrequestable, enforced by migration 0017 rather than by convention.
